prompt: Which HTTP status code should a REST API return when a user tries to access a resource they don't have permission to view?

options.text: 200 OK with an empty body
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found

hints: 401 = not authenticated. 403 = authenticated but not allowed. 404 = pretend it doesn't exist (also valid for security).
explanation: 403 Forbidden means: I know who you are, but you can't access this. 401 means: I don't know who you are yet. 404 is sometimes used deliberately to hide that a resource exists at all.

prompt:
Design a REST API for a Claude-powered writing tool. Define 3 endpoints:

1. `POST /api/generate` — generate text
2. `GET /api/history` — list past generations
3. `DELETE /api/history/:id` — delete one entry

For each endpoint write: method, path, request body/params, success response shape, and error cases.
hints: POST body: `{ prompt, tone, maxLength }`. Response: `{ id, result, createdAt }`
GET response: `{ items: [...], total, page }` (pagination from the start)
DELETE response: `{ success: true }` or 404 if not found
Error cases: 400 bad input, 401 not authenticated, 429 rate limited, 500 server error
explanation:
Good REST API design:
- POST /generate: body `{prompt}`, returns `{id, result, model, tokensUsed, createdAt}`
- GET /history: query params `?page=1&limit=20`, returns `{items:[...], total, hasMore}`
- DELETE /history/:id: returns `{success:true}` or 404 `{error:'Not found'}`
Consistency matters: always return JSON, always use the same error shape `{error: string}`.

prompt: Your Claude tool is getting popular and API costs are rising. What's the first optimization to try?

prompt: invoicelens's `/parse` endpoint returns `{ total: 412.50 }` for single-currency invoices and `{ amounts: { total: 412.50, currency: 'EUR' } }` for multi-currency ones, "to keep single-currency responses simple." What's the actual cost of this to an integrator building an unattended pipeline?

options.text: None — most invoices are single-currency, so most callers get the simple shape
Every caller now has to check which shape they got before reading the total, on every single response, forever
It's a documentation problem — clearly explaining the two shapes solves it
It only matters for the minority of multi-currency invoices, so it's a minor edge case

hints: An unattended pipeline can't have a human glance at the response and decide which shape it is.
"Most invoices are one shape" doesn't remove the need to handle the other shape — it just makes the bug rarer and harder to notice in testing.
explanation: The cost isn't proportional to how often the rare shape appears — it's paid on every response, by every integrator, because their code has no way to know in advance which shape it's about to receive without checking first. "Simple for most invoices" is actually "conditional for all invoices," since the conditional check has to run every time. Documentation can describe the two shapes but can't remove the branch every caller now has to write and maintain.

prompt: invoicelens's `confidence` field is a single number from 0 to 1. Support tickets show integrators can't tell whether a confidence of 0.4 means "the total was probably misread" or "the vendor name was probably misread" — the one number covers the whole invoice. Redesign the field so an integrator can tell, from the response alone, which specific extracted value to distrust. Write the new JSON shape and explain what problem it solves that the single number didn't.
hints: Think about what invoicelens actually extracts: vendor, total, date, line items — each one is a separate guess with its own uncertainty.
A shape like `confidence: { vendor: 0.9, total: 0.4, date: 0.95 }` lets a caller flag only the specific field that's shaky, instead of the whole invoice.
What should happen to line items, which are a list rather than a single value?
explanation: A workable shape: `{ vendor: { value, confidence }, total: { value, confidence }, date: { value, confidence }, lineItems: [{ value, confidence }, ...] }` — confidence attached per extracted field, not once for the whole document. This solves the actual problem: an integrator building an AP pipeline usually only needs a human to double-check the total (money) and can tolerate a shaky vendor spelling, but a single blended confidence number can't tell them which field to distrust. The single number was collapsing several independent judgments into one, exactly the pattern this lesson's diagnosis exercise identified with `total: null`.

prompt: invoicelens is renaming its four endpoints from actions to resource-based routes. Put these in the order a new integrator would most naturally discover and use them, and notice how the resource-based names make the sequence self-explanatory.

items: POST /api/invoices — submit a new invoice for parsing
GET /api/invoices/:id — fetch that invoice's parsed result
POST /api/invoices/:id/reparse — re-run extraction if the first pass looked wrong
DELETE /api/invoices/:id — remove the invoice's stored data when done with it

hints: You can't fetch, reparse, or delete an invoice that doesn't exist yet in the system.
Reparsing only makes sense after you've seen a first result you're unhappy with.
explanation: Create, then read, then (optionally) act on, then delete — the same lifecycle any resource-based API follows, which is exactly why naming around the resource (not the action) makes a new integrator's next move guessable instead of requiring a lookup in the docs for every step.

prompt: Match each invoicelens response situation to the status code that actually tells an automated caller what to do next.

pairs.left: The PDF is unreadable — corrupted file, will never parse no matter how many times it's retried
pairs.right: 422 Unprocessable Entity — don't retry, the content itself is the problem

pairs.left: The request JSON is missing the required `file` field
pairs.right: 400 Bad Request — fix the request shape before sending it again

pairs.left: The account's monthly invoice quota is used up
pairs.right: 402 Payment Required — needs a plan change or a human decision, not a retry

pairs.left: invoicelens's own parsing service threw an unexpected exception
pairs.right: 500 Internal Server Error — safe to retry once with backoff, it might be transient

pairs.left: The caller sent 50 requests in one second, past the rate limit
pairs.right: 429 Too Many Requests — retry after the delay in the Retry-After header

hints: Ask, for each row: if I retried this exact request unchanged, would the outcome ever be different?
A corrupt file and a missing field are both "this request failed," but only one of them can be fixed by changing what you send.
explanation: The dividing line every one of these status codes is drawing is retryability: 500 might resolve on its own (retry), 429 will resolve after a wait (retry later), but 400, 402, and 422 will produce the exact same failure forever unless something about the request, the account, or the file itself changes. Collapsing any of these into a generic 200-with-error-body, as invoicelens did with the corrupt PDF, removes that distinction and leaves automated callers guessing.

prompt: Sort each proposed change to invoicelens's API into breaking or non-breaking, using the test: would code written against the old behavior, unchanged, now do something different or fail?

items.text: Renaming `total` to `totalAmount`
Adding a new `currency` field alongside the existing fields
Changing `total` from pre-tax to post-tax, keeping the same field name
Adding a new `POST /invoices/:id/reparse` endpoint
Changing the default page size of `GET /invoices` from all results to 20 unless `?limit=` is passed
Accepting `.jpg` uploads in addition to the previously-required `.pdf`

hints: A field keeping its name but changing its meaning is one of the easiest breaking changes to miss in a code review — the diff looks small.
A default that changes silently changes what existing callers receive without any error being thrown.
explanation: The pre-tax-to-post-tax change is the sharpest trap here: the field name never changes, so a shape-diffing tool sees nothing different, but every integrator's stored numbers are now silently wrong. The default page-size change is the same pattern applied to a list endpoint — nothing about the request changed, but the response now quietly contains less data than before. Both are breaking for the same reason the sort-order example was: the danger is in changed *meaning* or *behavior*, not just changed *field names*.

prompt: Write invoicelens's actual rollout plan for retiring `total` in favor of `totalAmount` + `currency`. Include: what ships in v1 first, what the deprecation signal looks like on every affected response, how long the runway is and why, and what changes (if anything) in v2.
hints: Start with the additive step — what can ship immediately without breaking anyone?
A `Deprecation` and `Sunset` HTTP header on every v1 response using `total` tells automated clients (not just humans reading a changelog) that a change is coming.
The runway length should be long enough for the slowest-moving integrator to notice and act, not the fastest one.
explanation: A workable plan: (1) ship `totalAmount` and `currency` as new additive fields in v1 immediately — `total` keeps working unchanged; (2) add `Deprecation: true` and `Sunset: <date>` headers to every v1 response that still includes `total`, so automated monitoring (not just a human reading a changelog) can flag it; (3) give a runway of at least 90 days — long enough to catch integrators who only check their pipeline monthly; (4) email affected API keys directly (not just a general changelog) since that's the channel most likely to actually reach someone; (5) v2 is where `total` is finally removed — existing v1 callers are never forced to move, they simply lose access to a field they were already warned about, on a schedule they had months of notice for.

prompt: True or False: as long as every invoicelens endpoint returns a JSON error with *some* useful information in it, it doesn't matter whether the field names (`error` vs. `message`, an extra redundant `code` duplicating the status) are consistent across endpoints.

config.statement: As long as every invoicelens endpoint returns a JSON error with some useful information in it, it doesn't matter whether the field names are consistent across endpoints.
config.rubric: Full credit explains that inconsistent field names force an integrator to write one error handler per endpoint instead of one for the whole API, and that the cost compounds as the number of endpoints grows — the individual usefulness of each error's content doesn't offset that.

hints: Imagine writing one wrapper function meant to handle errors from every invoicelens endpoint at once.
"Useful per-endpoint" and "usable as a set" are two different properties.
explanation: False. Each endpoint's error might individually contain everything a human needs to understand what went wrong, but an integrator isn't reading errors one at a time by hand — they're writing code meant to handle errors from the whole API. Inconsistent shapes mean that code either becomes a pile of per-endpoint special cases, or it silently mishandles whichever endpoints don't match the shape it was written against. The cost isn't about any single error's content; it's about whether the *set* of all possible errors shares one predictable shape.

prompt: invoicelens wants to translate its error `message` field into French for European customers, without breaking anyone's error-handling code. Which design choice from this lesson makes that safe to do?

options.text: It's never safe — translating any part of an error response risks breaking integrators
Because integrators were told to branch on the stable `code` field, not the `message` text, translating message is exactly the kind of change the contract already allows
It's safe only if the translated message happens to be the same length as the English one
invoicelens should version-bump the API before translating any user-facing text

hints: Which field did this lesson explicitly say is not part of the stable contract?
A version bump is for changes to the contract itself — translating prose that was never part of the contract isn't one.
explanation: This is the entire payoff of separating `code` from `message`: because the documented contract only promises stability for `code` (and status, and `details`), changing `message` — including translating it — was never a breaking change in the first place. No version bump is needed because nothing that was promised to stay the same actually changed.

prompt: invoicelens's docs for the `error.code` field currently say: "code: a string identifying the error." Three integrators still email asking what codes exist. What's missing?

options.text: Nothing — the field's purpose is described accurately
A complete, enumerated list of every actual code the API can return, with the situation that produces each one
The docs should just link to the source code where errors are thrown
The field name should be changed to something clearer than `code`

hints: "A string identifying the error" describes the field's type and purpose, but not its actual possible values.
What would an integrator need in hand to write a complete switch statement covering every documented error before they've ever hit one in production?
explanation: Describing what a field *is for* isn't the same as documenting what values it can actually *take*. "A string identifying the error" is true but gives an integrator nothing to write code against — they'd have to trigger every error condition themselves just to discover the vocabulary. A full enumerated list (MISSING_FILE, VENDOR_NOT_FOUND, RATE_LIMITED, ...) with the situation and status code for each is what lets someone write complete error handling from the docs alone, matching this lesson's build-it exercise.

prompt: Design invoicelens's process for keeping the `GET /invoices/:id` doc's example response accurate forever, without anyone having to remember to update it by hand. Be concrete: what runs, when, and what happens if the API's real response no longer matches what's documented.
hints: Where should the example response text actually come from — hand-typed, or captured from a real call?
What should happen in CI if a route change makes the generated example different from what's committed in the docs?
Think about who should see that mismatch, and when — before merge, or after an integrator reports it?
explanation: A workable process: a fixture invoice lives in the test suite; a script calls the real (test-environment) `/invoices/:id` endpoint against it and writes the response directly into the docs as a generated code block, run as part of CI on every pull request touching the invoices route. If a route change alters the response shape, the generated block changes too, showing up as a diff in that same pull request — the reviewer sees the doc update alongside the code change, in the same review, rather than the two drifting apart silently. No separate reminder, checklist item, or docs-repo owner is required, because the example is mechanically incapable of going stale without the CI diff making it visible first.

prompt: invoicelens adds `POST /api/invoices/delete/:id` to remove an invoice. What's the naming defect, and what should it be instead?

options.text: It's fine — the URL clearly says what it does
The verb `delete` is in the URL; it should be `DELETE /api/invoices/:id`, letting the HTTP verb carry the action
It should be `GET /api/invoices/delete/:id` instead, since deleting doesn't need a body
The `:id` should come before `delete` in the path

hints: Which part of this URL is redundant with something HTTP already gives you for free?
explanation: `delete` in the path duplicates what the `DELETE` HTTP verb already means — the resource-based version is `DELETE /api/invoices/:id`, consistent with how the module named the other three endpoints.

prompt: True or False: returning `200 OK` for a request that failed validation is fine as long as the response body clearly says `{ "success": false }`.

config.statement: Returning 200 OK for a request that failed validation is fine as long as the response body clearly says success: false.
config.rubric: Full credit explains that automated infrastructure (retry logic, monitoring, load balancers) makes decisions based on the status code first, and a 200 promises success regardless of what the body underneath it says.

hints: Who reads the status code before the body — a human, or a piece of infrastructure?
explanation: False, for the same reason the corrupt-PDF retry loop never stopped in this module's second lesson: automated systems trust the status code as the first signal, and `200` tells every one of them "this succeeded," no matter what the body says underneath.

prompt: Which of these is a breaking change to invoicelens's API, using the test "would code written against the old behavior now do something different or fail"?

options.text: Adding a new `GET /invoices/:id/audit-log` endpoint
Changing line items from an unordered array to always sorted by page number
Adding an optional `?format=csv` query parameter to an existing endpoint
Accepting `.heic` uploads in addition to the previously-required `.pdf`/`.jpg`

hints: Three of these four only add capability without touching anything that already worked.
explanation: The sort-order change is breaking precisely because it's silent — nothing is renamed or removed, but any integrator relying on the array's previous order (even unintentionally) now gets different results with no error. The other three are purely additive: new endpoint, new optional param, and a widened set of accepted inputs, none of which affect a caller who doesn't opt in.

prompt: Match each HTTP status code to the situation invoicelens should use it for.

pairs.right: The API key is missing or invalid
The account's quota or billing is blocking the request
The request was well-formed, but the file's content couldn't be parsed
The caller exceeded the rate limit

hints: Two of these are about who's asking and whether they're allowed to; two are about what happens once the request goes through.
explanation: 401 and 402 are about the caller's standing (identity, billing); 422 and 429 are about what happened once a legitimate request was processed — content that can't be parsed, or too many requests too fast. Mixing these up (e.g. using 400 for a billing issue) hides the real cause from automated monitoring built to distinguish them.

prompt: True or False: a field that's usually present but occasionally missing should simply be omitted from the JSON response, rather than included with a value of `null`.

config.statement: A field that's usually present but occasionally missing should simply be omitted from the JSON response, rather than included with a value of null.
config.rubric: Full credit explains that omission makes response shape depend on the input (the module 1 lesson's core problem), forcing every caller to check whether a key exists at all rather than reading one predictable shape.

hints: Recall the two competing invoice-extraction APIs from the first lesson — what made one buildable against and the other not?
explanation: False. Omitting a field when it's absent means the response shape itself now varies by input — exactly the API-A problem from this module's first lesson. Keeping the key with a `null` value keeps the shape identical on every response; a caller checks one thing (`response.total === null`) instead of first checking whether `total` exists at all.

prompt: Sort each proposed invoicelens API change into breaking or non-breaking.

items.text: Renaming a field
Adding a new optional field to an existing response
Changing the set of valid values an existing enum field can hold
Adding a brand-new endpoint
Changing a list endpoint's default sort order
Tightening validation to reject an input that used to be silently accepted

hints: A validation change that used to let something through and now rejects it will break any caller whose input relied on that leniency.
explanation: Tightening validation is the one easy to miss: it feels like a bug fix, but if any existing integrator was (even accidentally) relying on the old, looser behavior, their previously-working requests now fail. Combined with the enum and sort-order cases, the pattern holds: anything that changes what a caller who did nothing differently now experiences is breaking, regardless of whether it looks like an improvement.

prompt: invoicelens's error `code` field should be built from which of these?

options.text: A stable, documented enum string like `VENDOR_NOT_FOUND`, committed to never changing meaning once published
The raw `error.message` text from whatever exception was thrown internally
The HTTP status code repeated as a string, e.g. `"404"`
A random request ID, so each error is uniquely traceable

hints: What did this module's lesson on error contracts say was the one field integrators were told is safe to branch on?
explanation: A raw exception message changes wording whenever a developer touches the code that throws it — exactly the fragility that broke the integrator's string-matching logic in this module's error-contract lesson. A stable, documented enum is the one thing an API can actually promise won't change out from under a caller's branching logic.

prompt: Put these steps of safely retiring the deprecated `total` field in order.

items: Ship `totalAmount` and `currency` as new additive fields while `total` keeps working unchanged
Add `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers to every response still including `total`
Give a runway of at least 90 days and notify affected API keys directly
Remove `total` only in a new API version that existing v1 callers are never forced onto

hints: The field has to exist before anything can be marked deprecated in a response header.
Removal is the very last step, and only in a version nobody is forced onto.
explanation: Additive first (nothing breaks yet), then a machine-readable deprecation signal on every affected response, then a real runway with direct notification (not just a changelog, per this module's prediction exercise on how few integrators read one), and only then removal — and even then, only in a version existing callers were never forced onto.

prompt: invoicelens's founder wants to add a card-number input field on their own site and POST it to their own `/api/charge` endpoint before forwarding it to a payments provider. What's the actual problem with this plan?

options.text: Nothing — as long as the card number is forwarded immediately and never stored, it's fine
The moment the card number reaches invoicelens's own server, that server is in PCI DSS scope, triggering ongoing compliance obligations regardless of how briefly the data is held
It's only a problem if invoicelens later gets breached
The only real fix is switching to a different payments provider

hints: PCI scope is triggered by data merely passing through a server, not just by storing it.
"Forward it immediately" doesn't change whether the data touched the server at all.
explanation: PCI DSS scope is triggered by a server processing or transmitting card data — not just storing it. Even a millisecond of the card number passing through invoicelens's own endpoint before forwarding it puts that server under the same compliance obligations as one that stores card numbers permanently. The fix is architectural (never receive the number at all, via a hosted checkout or embedded widget), not procedural ("be careful with it").

prompt: True or False: since invoicelens's developer already knows how to securely hash and store passwords, storing encrypted card numbers themselves (instead of using a payments provider) is a reasonable, comparably-sized engineering task.

config.statement: Since invoicelens's developer already knows how to securely hash and store passwords, storing encrypted card numbers themselves is a reasonable, comparably-sized engineering task.
config.rubric: Full credit explains that passwords need one-way, non-reversible verification while card numbers need to be reversibly recoverable to charge again, making this a different and harder problem with regulatory liability attached, not a bigger version of the same skill.

hints: What does a password hash need to do that's fundamentally different from what a stored card number needs to do?
explanation: False. Password hashing is one-way by design — you never need the original password back, only a way to verify a guess against it. A stored card number has to be reversible enough to actually charge the card again later, which is a fundamentally different (and much higher-liability) engineering problem, not a scaled-up version of password hashing.

prompt: Write the `stripe.checkout.sessions.create()` call for invoicelens's Team plan (a different price than Pro). It needs to pass through which invoicelens user is subscribing and which plan they chose, so the webhook handler can later upgrade the correct account correctly. Include the metadata your webhook handler would need to read.
hints: mode: 'subscription' for a recurring plan, line_items pointing at the Team price ID.
metadata is a flat object of strings — invoicelensUserId and plan are the two pieces of information the webhook handler will need later.
success_url and cancel_url still matter even though the webhook (not the redirect) does the actual account upgrade — they control what the user sees.

prompt: A user starts invoicelens's Pro checkout, closes the tab without paying, and comes back four days later through a bookmarked Stripe link to finish. What does invoicelens's server know about this, in real time, while it's happening?

options.text: Nothing — the server has no visibility into what happens on Stripe's hosted page until it's told afterward
It can see the user is mid-checkout via a live session status endpoint it should be polling
The four-day gap causes the Checkout session to silently fail, so this scenario can't actually happen
invoicelens's frontend maintains an open connection to Stripe's page that reports progress

hints: What does your server actually control once the browser has been redirected to a different domain?
explanation: Once the browser is redirected to Stripe's hosted page, your server has handed off entirely — there's no live connection, no polling endpoint being watched, nothing. Checkout sessions do have an expiration (commonly 24 hours by default, configurable), but within that window the server genuinely has zero visibility into what the user is doing until Stripe reports back, which is exactly why the redirect back to your site isn't a reliable signal on its own — the next lesson explains why.

prompt: True or False: it's fine for invoicelens's `success_url` page to be the one that calls the code granting a user their Pro plan access, as long as it also double-checks with Stripe's API that a payment actually happened before granting it.

config.statement: It's fine for the success_url page to grant Pro plan access, as long as it double-checks with Stripe's API that a payment actually happened first.
config.rubric: Full credit recognizes that the redirect itself isn't proof, but a server-side check against Stripe's API (not just trusting the query string) makes this safe — while noting the webhook is still needed as a backstop for users who never return to complete the redirect at all.

hints: The problem in this lesson wasn't that success_url ran code — it was that it trusted the browser's presence on the URL as proof.
What happens to a user who pays but closes the tab before the redirect ever fires?
explanation: True, with a real caveat: checking Stripe's API server-side (not trusting the query string) removes the forgery risk from this lesson's diagnosis exercise. But it can't be the *only* mechanism — a user who pays and closes the tab before the redirect completes would never trigger this check at all, which is exactly the gap a webhook (a server-to-server event Stripe sends regardless of what the user's browser does next) exists to close. In practice, most teams skip the redirect-side check entirely and rely on the webhook alone, since it covers both cases with one mechanism.

prompt: invoicelens's webhook handler uses `express.json()` (the standard JSON body parser) before `stripe.webhooks.constructEvent()`. Signature verification starts failing on every real event from Stripe. Why?

options.text: express.json() parses and re-serializes the body, so the bytes constructEvent checks the signature against no longer match what Stripe originally signed
express.json() is incompatible with Stripe's SDK entirely and should never be used anywhere in the same app
The webhook secret must have been rotated on Stripe's dashboard
Signature verification only works over HTTPS, and this server is running on HTTP

hints: Stripe computes the signature over the exact raw bytes of the request body it sent — what happens to those bytes once a JSON parser has already touched them?
explanation: Stripe signs the literal raw bytes of the webhook payload. Once `express.json()` parses that body into a JavaScript object and Express (or your code) re-serializes it, even formatting differences like key order or whitespace change the bytes — and a signature computed over different bytes will never match. This is exactly why the webhook route needs `express.raw({ type: 'application/json' })` specifically for that one path, applied before any general JSON body-parsing middleware.

prompt: Put invoicelens's handling of a failed renewal charge in the correct order, from the charge failing to what should happen if it's never resolved.

items: Renewal charge fails because the customer's card expired
invoicelens's invoice.payment_failed handler emails the customer with a link to update their card; access stays active
Stripe automatically retries the charge over roughly the next two weeks
If a retry succeeds, access simply continues uninterrupted with no further action needed
If all retries fail, Stripe fires customer.subscription.deleted and invoicelens downgrades the account, with an email explaining why

hints: Access loss should be the last resort, only after retries are genuinely exhausted, not the immediate response to the first failure.
explanation: The sequence gives an innocent, common cause (an expired card) a real chance to self-resolve — through Stripe's automatic retries and a customer who's been actually told what happened — before access is ever removed, and removal itself is still explained by email rather than silent.

prompt: invoicelens receives a `charge.dispute.created` webhook for a customer who claims they never authorized a Pro-plan charge, but invoicelens's logs show that account making 4,000 API calls that same billing period. Design the process invoicelens should follow between receiving this webhook and the dispute's response deadline. What gets gathered, and what gets submitted?
hints: What evidence would actually counter a claim of "I never authorized this" — proof the service was delivered and used, and proof the customer agreed to be charged.
The response has a hard deadline — what needs to happen automatically the moment the webhook fires, versus what a human has time to do later within the window?
Think about what Stripe's dispute-evidence submission actually accepts: usage logs, signed terms, prior correspondence.
explanation: A workable process: the webhook immediately creates an internal ticket with the dispute's deadline attached (so it can't be silently missed), and flags — but does not yet cancel — the account. A human gathers evidence before the deadline: the account's API usage logs for that billing period (4,000 calls is strong evidence the service was used, not unauthorized), the signup record showing terms-of-service acceptance and the original checkout confirmation, and any prior support correspondence with that customer. That evidence gets submitted through Stripe's dispute-evidence API before the deadline. This is different from a plain refund in exactly the way this lesson's evidence-stack exercise distinguished them: there's a hard deadline, a fee regardless of outcome, and a real burden of proof — not a one-click reversal.

prompt: invoicelens's Stripe secret key is stored correctly in an environment variable and was never committed to git. It still turned up in an error-tracking dashboard. What actually happened?

options.text: Environment variables aren't a secure enough place to store secrets
General error logging captured the full failing request, including a header a library had attached, with nothing configured to redact it first
The Stripe SDK has a known bug that leaks its own secret key
This can only happen if the .env file itself was accidentally deployed publicly

hints: "Never committed to git" and "never logged anywhere" are two separate disciplines.
explanation: Avoiding git is only one leak path closed. Verbose error/request logging is a separate path a secret can travel through entirely independent of version control — and unless the logging layer specifically redacts sensitive headers before persisting anything, a library-attached Authorization header rides along with everything else a crash report captures.

prompt: True or False: logging `console.log(event)` for the full Stripe webhook payload is a reasonable debugging step, since the last-four card digits it contains aren't the full card number and aren't PCI-scoped data on their own.

config.statement: Logging the full Stripe webhook payload is reasonable for debugging, since the last-four card digits it contains aren't the full card number and aren't PCI-scoped on their own.
config.rubric: Full credit explains that last-four digits combined with name, email, and billing address in a general-purpose log (weaker access controls and retention discipline than the payments provider's own dashboard) still constitutes real customer PII, even though it isn't literally PCI-scoped card data.

hints: Not being PCI-scoped and being safe to log anywhere are two different claims.
What else is sitting in that same log line alongside the last-four digits?
explanation: False. Being technically outside PCI's strictest scope doesn't mean the data is harmless to log — last-four digits, combined with the customer's name, email, and billing address in the same event object, form a real piece of financial and personal identity, now sitting in general server logs with weaker access controls and longer, less deliberate retention than the payments provider's own dashboard already gives that same information. The fix is logging only the event type and ID, never the full payload.

prompt: A developer proposes handling card numbers in-house because "we already store hashed passwords securely." What's the actual flaw in that reasoning?

options.text: Password hashing is one-way; a stored card number must be reversible enough to charge again, which is a different, higher-liability problem
There's no real flaw — the skills genuinely transfer
Card numbers are simply longer than passwords, requiring a bigger database column
Password hashing and card storage both require the exact same PCI certification

hints: What does a password hash need to do that a stored card number can't do?
explanation: One-way verification (passwords) and reversible reuse (card numbers) are fundamentally different requirements — the reasoning fails because it treats a category difference as a scale difference.

prompt: True or False: as long as a card number is forwarded to a payments provider within milliseconds and never stored, the server it briefly passed through is outside PCI DSS scope.

config.statement: As long as a card number is forwarded to a payments provider within milliseconds and never stored, the server it briefly passed through is outside PCI DSS scope.
config.rubric: Full credit explains PCI scope is triggered by processing or transmitting card data, not only by storing it — brief transit still counts.

hints: Re-read this module's first lesson: what three things trigger PCI scope, not just one?
explanation: False. PCI DSS scope covers storing, processing, *or transmitting* card data — a server that only ever forwards the number for a millisecond has still processed and transmitted it, which is enough to trigger scope regardless of storage duration.

prompt: invoicelens needs to attach a specific plan and user ID to each checkout so the webhook handler knows whose account to upgrade. Which integration option makes that straightforward without taking on custom card-form validation?

A fully custom embedded card form
None of these can carry metadata — it has to be reconstructed after the fact

hints: Which option lets you set metadata at session-creation time without owning the card form's UI and validation?
explanation: Hosted Checkout is created through a backend API call, which is exactly where metadata like the user ID and plan can be attached — giving invoicelens what it needs without the cost of building and maintaining a fully custom card form.

prompt: Put these steps of an invoicelens Checkout flow in the order they actually happen.

items: Backend creates a Checkout session with user ID and plan in metadata
Frontend redirects the browser to the session's hosted URL
User completes payment on Stripe's page, invisible to invoicelens's server
Stripe sends a signature-verified webhook event to invoicelens's server
The webhook handler reads the metadata and upgrades the correct account

hints: The session has to exist before there's anywhere to redirect to.
The account upgrade happens in the webhook handler, not in the redirect back to your site.
explanation: This is the same sequence from the module's lessons: create, redirect, invisible payment, webhook, upgrade — the webhook, not the browser redirect, is what actually triggers the account change.

prompt: True or False: it's safe to grant Pro access the moment a user's browser lands on the success_url page, as long as the URL includes a long, hard-to-guess random token.

config.statement: It's safe to grant access based on the browser landing on success_url, as long as the URL includes a long, hard-to-guess random token.
config.rubric: Full credit explains that a token is still something the browser (fully user-controlled) can possess and replay — the actual fix is a server-to-server, signature-verified webhook, not a harder-to-guess URL.

hints: Who controls what URL the browser is sitting on, regardless of how random the token in it is?
explanation: False. A random token changes what's needed to construct the URL, but not the underlying problem — the browser's location is still fully user-controlled information, not a server-verified fact. The actual fix is granting access only from a signature-verified webhook, which the user's browser cannot forge or replay.

prompt: invoicelens's webhook handler starts failing signature verification on every real Stripe event after a refactor. The most likely cause, given this module's lessons?

options.text: Stripe's webhook secret is rotated automatically every few days
A general JSON body-parser now runs before the webhook route, re-serializing the body so its bytes no longer match what Stripe originally signed
The server's clock has drifted out of sync
The webhook URL changed and Stripe is sending events to the old one

hints: What does signature verification actually check the signature against — the parsed object, or the raw bytes?
explanation: This is the exact failure mode this module's third lesson walked through: signature verification needs the untouched raw request body, and a general JSON body-parser running first destroys that by parsing and re-serializing it before it reaches the Stripe SDK's verification call.

prompt: Match each Stripe webhook event to what invoicelens should actually do when it fires.

Email the customer to update their card; keep access active during the retry window
Downgrade access, only after Stripe's retries are genuinely exhausted
Start a deadline-tracked evidence-gathering process, not a simple refund

hints: Two of these are about payment succeeding or failing; two are about a subscription actually ending versus a formal dispute.
explanation: Each event answers a genuinely different question, and treating any two of them as interchangeable is exactly what caused the problems earlier in this module — silent renewal failures, sudden access loss with no warning, and missed dispute deadlines.

prompt: A debugging session adds `console.log(event)` to invoicelens's webhook handler, logging the full Stripe event object. What's the actual risk, even though no full card number is included?

options.text: None — without a full card number, nothing sensitive is being logged
Last-four digits combined with name, email, and billing address in one log line still constitute real customer PII, now sitting in a system with weaker protections than Stripe's own dashboard
console.log is inherently insecure and should never be used, even for non-sensitive values
The risk only applies in production, not during local development

hints: What else is riding along in the same object as the last-four digits?
explanation: Not being full PCI-scoped card data doesn't mean the combined fields are harmless — last-four digits plus name, email, and address is real personal and financial identity information, now persisted in general server logs with weaker access control and retention discipline than the payments provider's own dashboard already provides for that same data.

prompt: invoicelens's dashboard shows rising signups, rising API call volume, and rising page views — the same month MRR quietly starts falling. What does this actually reveal about the tracked metrics?

options.text: The metrics are lying or broken somehow
All four tracked numbers measure volume arriving at the top of the funnel, none of them measure whether existing paying users are staying and finding value
MRR is simply a lagging indicator that will eventually catch up to the other trends
This combination of numbers is actually impossible and indicates a tracking bug

hints: Ask what each of the four rising numbers is actually counting — arrivals, or ongoing engagement.
explanation: None of the four numbers were ever built to measure retention or paying-user health — they're all volume-at-the-top-of-funnel metrics. It's entirely possible, and not a bug, for new visitors to keep arriving while existing paying customers quietly churn underneath that growth, since nothing in the tracked set was watching for that.

prompt: invoicelens's numbers: 1,000 signups, 100 activated (uploaded an invoice and got a result), 70 of those 100 still active in week 4, and healthy revenue among the paying subset. A teammate wants to A/B test three different pricing pages to "grow revenue." Explain, using this lesson's ordering, why that's not the highest-leverage place to start — and where is.
hints: Which of the three core metrics (activation, retention, revenue) is the bottleneck here, based on the actual numbers?
Can revenue improve for a user who never got a first successful result at all?
What's the actual leverage of fixing a number that's already healthy for the population it applies to, versus a number that's failing for 90% of everyone who arrives?
explanation: Revenue and retention both look strong, but only among the 10% who ever activated — pricing-page experiments would only ever reach that already-healthy slice, since the other 900 users never got far enough to see a pricing page in a context where it mattered. The highest-leverage fix is upstream: find out what's failing between signup and first successful invoice upload for the 900 who never activated. Improving activation from 10% to even 20% would roughly double the population retention and revenue could ever apply to — a bigger structural win than optimizing pricing copy for an already-small, already-converting group.

prompt: Sort each candidate invoicelens event into worth tracking or noise, using the test: would a change in this number next week point at a specific action to take?

items.text: invoice_upload_failed, with a reason enum
mouse_x_position on the upload page
quota_limit_hit, with plan and limit type
css_animation_completed on a loading spinner
plan_cancelled, with tenure and previous plan
page_scroll_percentage on the marketing homepage

hints: A spike in mouse position or scroll percentage doesn't point at a fixable action the way a spike in upload failures does.
explanation: The three "worth tracking" events each map to a real, specific product question (why do uploads fail, who's hitting limits and might upgrade, who's leaving and from what plan). The three "noise" events are technically capturable but a spike in any of them doesn't suggest a next action — nobody changes their roadmap because scroll percentage moved.

prompt: True or False: logging `invoice_upload_failed` with a free-text `errorMessage` string (whatever the exception happened to say) is just as useful as logging it with a fixed `reason` enum.

config.statement: Logging invoice_upload_failed with a free-text errorMessage string is just as useful as logging it with a fixed reason enum.
config.rubric: Full credit explains that free-text messages can change wording over time (from a code refactor or copy tweak) making grouped counting unreliable, while a fixed enum stays queryable regardless of message wording changes.

hints: Recall the API-design module's distinction between a stable error `code` and free-text `message` — the same logic applies to analytics properties.
explanation: False. A free-text message is whatever the underlying exception happened to say at the time, and it can change wording the next time someone touches that code path — silently splitting what should be one countable category into several differently-worded ones, or merging it invisibly with an unrelated failure. A fixed `reason` enum (`unsupported_format`, `corrupt_file`, `timeout`) stays reliably groupable no matter how the human-facing message text evolves.

prompt: invoicelens knows 90% of signups never activate, but has no idea which step of the signup-to-first-result journey loses the most people. What does building a step-by-step funnel add that the single 90% number doesn't have?

options.text: Nothing new — it's the same 90% expressed differently
A count at each discrete step, showing exactly where in the sequence the biggest single drop-off happens, instead of one blended total
A funnel is mainly useful for comparing invoicelens against competitors
It replaces the need for the activation event entirely

hints: What does the 90% number tell you, and what does it not tell you, about where in the journey people are stopping?
explanation: The 90% figure only tells you *that* a large drop-off exists between two endpoints. A funnel breaks that same drop-off into per-step counts, revealing which specific step — in invoicelens's case, the verification email — accounts for the largest share, which is the only version of this information that actually points at where to spend effort.

prompt: invoicelens's upload flow renders five separate pages (file picker, preview, confirm, processing, result) but represents only two real decisions (commit to uploading, get an outcome). Redesign the funnel's step list to reflect real decision boundaries instead of page loads, and explain what would have been hidden by tracking all five pages as separate steps.
hints: Which of the five pages are really just different views of the same not-yet-committed decision?
What single moment counts as "the user has actually committed to uploading"?
If the confirm page has an unusually confusing button, what would happen to that signal if it's buried inside a five-step funnel versus a two-step one?
explanation: A corrected funnel: account_created → verification_email_clicked → committed_to_upload (the moment a file is chosen and submit is clicked, regardless of how many preview/confirm screens preceded it) → got_a_result. Tracking all five pages separately would dilute any real problem — say, a confusing confirm button costing a 15% drop — across two or three page-to-page transitions that each look individually minor, when collapsed into one "committed_to_upload" step that same 15% would show up as one unmistakable number pointing straight at that part of the flow.

prompt: True or False: logging the full extracted text of a customer's invoice into invoicelens's analytics platform is acceptable as long as it's only used internally for debugging, never shared externally.

config.statement: Logging the full extracted text of a customer's invoice into the analytics platform is acceptable as long as it's only used internally for debugging.
config.rubric: Full credit explains the data has moved into a third-party system without the access controls, retention limits, or contractual obligations that were designed for it, regardless of internal-only intent — and that the content belongs to invoicelens's customer's own client, a third party who never consented to this at all.

hints: Who does the invoice actually belong to, and did they agree to their data landing in a third-party analytics vendor?
Does "internal use only" change which system the data is physically sitting in, or just who's allowed to look at it there?
explanation: False. "Internal only" describes an intended use, not where the data actually lives or what protections apply to it there — the invoice content is now inside a third-party analytics vendor with none of the access controls or retention limits that were designed with confidential documents in mind, and it belongs to invoicelens's customer's own client, someone who never consented to any of this. Good intent about internal use doesn't change the actual exposure.

prompt: invoicelens's cookie banner has a large "Accept" button and a tiny grey "reject" link styled to blend into the background. Legally, both options exist. What's actually wrong with this design?

options.text: Nothing — offering both options satisfies the legal requirement
A reject option that's deliberately harder to find or use than accept isn't real consent — it's the same tracking with an extra, mostly-ignorable step added
The banner should be removed entirely to avoid the issue
The problem is only the color choice, not the underlying design pattern

hints: What's the actual difference between "a choice exists" and "a choice is genuinely offered"?
explanation: Technically offering a reject option that's styled to be missed produces the same outcome as not offering one at all for the vast majority of users, who click the obvious button without noticing an alternative. Genuine consent requires both options to be equally visible and equally easy to act on — the design pattern itself, not just the specific colors used, is what makes this dishonest.

prompt: Put invoicelens's iteration cycle in order, from noticing the verification-email drop-off to knowing whether the fix worked.

items: Notice the verification-click rate is 60%, in the weekly data review
Form a specific hypothesis: adding a resend-email button should raise it to 75%+ within two weeks
Build the smallest version of that change — just the resend button, nothing else
Measure the click rate again after exactly the two-week window
Keep the change if it moved as predicted, revert or iterate if it didn't

hints: The hypothesis has to name a specific number and a specific window before the change ships, not after.
explanation: The hypothesis step is what separates this from the passive three-month habit in this lesson's first pod — committing in advance to what success looks like and by when is what makes step 5 (keep or revert) an actual decision instead of another vague impression.

prompt: invoicelens's funnel shows 15% of committed uploads fail, 60% of those are unsupported-format, and most of those are .heic files. Before deciding whether to build full .heic parsing support, what one additional piece of data would most change the decision, and why?
hints: Is the .heic failure rate broad and steady across many different customers, or could it be one customer's unusual onboarding batch skewing the whole number?
What would change about the cost-benefit if this turned out to be a one-time cluster versus an ongoing pattern?
explanation: The most decision-changing follow-up is whether the .heic failures are spread across many distinct customers over time, or concentrated in one or two accounts during a single onboarding period. If it's broad and sustained, full .heic support is a real, generalizable fix worth the engineering cost. If it's one customer's batch upload of iPhone photos during a single week, a format warning (cheap, immediate) plus a direct conversation with that customer is a better-targeted response than building permanent parsing infrastructure for what might be an unusual, non-representative case.

prompt: A dashboard shows rising signups and rising page views. Which additional metric would actually tell you whether the paying user base is healthy?

Week-over-week retention among users who already activated
Average session duration on the marketing homepage
Total number of blog posts published

hints: Which of these actually measures whether existing users are staying, versus how many new visitors are arriving?
explanation: Retention is the one metric here that measures whether people who already found the product are still finding it valuable — the others are all top-of-funnel or marketing-adjacent numbers that can rise while paying users quietly leave.

prompt: True or False: a healthy retention number, on its own, proves that activation isn't a problem.

config.statement: A healthy retention number, on its own, proves that activation isn't a problem.

hints: Retention is measured among which population — everyone who signed up, or everyone who already got through activation?
explanation: False. Retention is calculated only among users who already activated — it says nothing about the (possibly much larger) group who never got that far. A tool can have excellent retention among a tiny surviving population while activation quietly fails for 90% of everyone who signs up.

prompt: Which of these events is worth adding to a tracking plan, by the test "would a change in this number point at a specific action"?

quota_limit_hit, with plan and limit type as properties
button_color_rendered on page load
total_css_files_loaded

hints: Which one, if it spiked next week, would tell you exactly who to look at and why?

prompt: Sort each property choice for an upload_failed event into good practice or a mistake to avoid.

items.text: A fixed reason enum like 'corrupt_file' or 'unsupported_format'
The raw exception message text, whatever it happened to say
The file type that failed to upload
The full extracted text content of the failed document

hints: One of these mistakes is about query reliability over time; the other is about capturing sensitive content that doesn't belong in analytics.
explanation: A stable reason enum and a file type are both queryable, specific, and don't carry sensitive content. Free-text exception messages drift in wording and become unreliable to group; full document content is exactly the kind of sensitive data this module's privacy lesson said doesn't belong in a third-party analytics platform.

prompt: True or False: breaking a two-endpoint drop-off number into a five-page funnel, with one step per page load, is always more useful than a shorter funnel of real decision points.

config.statement: Breaking a drop-off number into a step per page load is always more useful than a shorter funnel built from real decision points.
config.rubric: Full credit explains that fragmenting one real decision across several near-identical page-load steps dilutes the signal rather than sharpening it.

hints: What happened to the 40% verification-email drop-off signal when it was buried inside a longer chain of near-identical page-load steps?
explanation: False. A funnel step should represent a real decision or outcome; splitting one decision into several page-load steps dilutes drop-off across steps that all really measure the same underlying moment, making the actual signal harder to see, not easier.

prompt: A developer wants to log a customer's full document text into a third-party analytics platform "in case it's useful later." What's the right response, per this module's filter?

options.text: Ask whether you'd be comfortable explaining exactly what this event captures, in plain language, to the person whose data it is — and only log it if the answer is genuinely yes
Log it — more data is always more useful eventually
Only log it if the analytics vendor promises not to look at it
Log a hash of the document instead of the raw text

hints: Recall the plain-language explanation test from this module's privacy lesson.
explanation: The plain-language test cuts through "might be useful later" directly — if you can't comfortably say out loud exactly what's being captured and why to the person it belongs to, it's a signal the data doesn't belong where it's headed. A hash still means moving something derived from confidential content into a system that wasn't built or contracted to hold it.

prompt: Put the steps of turning an observed metric into an actual, checkable decision in order.

Build the smallest version of that change
Measure again after exactly the stated window
